title: Air Masses, Fronts and Temperate Cyclones

cards.h: Weather in mid-latitudes is a story of collisions
cards.b: A huge body of air takes on the heat and moisture of the surface beneath it. When two such bodies meet, they make a front and a storm. This lesson links to western disturbances in India, to Europe's weather and to winter rain in the Mediterranean. It is a steady source of conceptual questions.

An air mass is a large body of air, often 1,600 km or more across, with nearly uniform temperature and humidity at any height. It forms over a source region that is flat, uniform and under light winds: the polar ice, the Sahara, the warm oceans.

Names use two letters. First: c continental (dry) or m maritime (moist). Second: T tropical, P polar, A arctic, E equatorial.

mT maritime tropical: warm, moist, over warm oceans. cT continental tropical: hot, dry, over deserts. mP maritime polar: cool and moist. cP continental polar: cold and dry. cA continental arctic: very cold, from the ice sheets.

Indian monsoon is driven by mE (maritime equatorial) air flowing in from the southern Indian Ocean.

A front is the sloping boundary between two unlike air masses. The warmer, lighter air rises over the colder, denser air. This lifting makes cloud and rain.

  • Cold front: cold air pushes under warm. Steep slope, short heavy rain, thunder.
  • Warm front: warm air slides over cold. Gentle slope, long steady drizzle.
  • Stationary front: neither moves.
  • Occluded front: a cold front catches a warm front.

The creation of a front is frontogenesis. Its decay is frontolysis. The main global front is the polar front, where cold polar easterlies meet warm westerlies near 60 degrees N and S.

The Norwegian meteorologist Vilhelm Bjerknes and colleagues developed the polar front theory around 1918-1920. 'Front' was chosen by analogy with the battle fronts of World War I.

A temperate (extratropical) cyclone grows along the polar front through stages: initial, incipient, mature, occlusion and dissipation. A wave forms on the front. Warm air flows into a pocket, called the warm sector, between a cold and a warm front. Pressure falls at the centre. The cold front moves faster and eventually overtakes the warm front. The cyclone then dies.

Tropical cyclones are smaller (100-500 km), form only over warm seas above about 26.5 degrees C, have an eye, and weaken over land. Temperate cyclones are much larger (up to 2,000 km), can form over land or sea, have no eye, move west to east with the westerlies, and have fronts.

Tropical ones have a warm core. Temperate ones have a cold core in the upper air and are driven by temperature contrast.

An anticyclone is a high-pressure system: clear skies, light winds, dry weather. Winds blow clockwise in the north and anticlockwise in the south. It brings summer heat and winter cold waves.

When an anticyclone stalls for days, it blocks the usual westerly flow and causes heatwaves or floods nearby, such as the European heatwave of 2003.

The western disturbance is an extratropical storm born over the Mediterranean and carried east by the subtropical westerly jet. It brings winter rain to northwest India and snow to the Himalaya. Cold fronts also help produce cold waves in Punjab and Haryana. Air mass thinking explains the monsoon too: the arrival of mE air.

Likely questions: 'Differentiate tropical and temperate cyclones', 'Explain the formation of fronts', 'Role of air masses in weather'.

  • Use a table with five rows: origin, size, eye, movement, season.
  • Draw a warm sector with the two fronts.
  • Link to western disturbances for the Indian marks.
